claim: Neuropathic pain following peripheral nerve injury is associated with hyperexcitability in damaged myelinated sensory axons.
source: Neuropathic pain following peripheral nerve injury is associated with hyperexcitability in damaged myelinated sensory axons, which begins to normalise over time.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that forms the basis for the study.

claim: Hyperexcitability in damaged myelinated sensory axons begins to normalise over time.
source: Neuropathic pain following peripheral nerve injury is associated with hyperexcitability in damaged myelinated sensory axons, which begins to normalise over time.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon.

claim: At the neuroma that forms after damage, expression of Kv1.1 and 1.2 was markedly decreased.
source: At the neuroma that forms after damage, expression of Kv1.1 and 1.2 (normally localised to the juxtaparanode) was markedly decreased.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Western blot and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Kv1.1 and 1.2 are normally localised to the juxtaparanode.
source: At the neuroma that forms after damage, expression of Kv1.1 and 1.2 (normally localised to the juxtaparanode) was markedly decreased.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Kv1.4 and 1.6 were hardly detectable in the naïve state.
source: In contrast Kv1.4 and 1.6, which were hardly detectable in the naïve state, showed increased expression within juxtaparanodes and paranodes following injury, both in rats and humans.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry and Western blot data in Figure 1.

claim: Kv1.4 and 1.6 showed increased expression within juxtaparanodes and paranodes following injury in rats.
source: In contrast Kv1.4 and 1.6, which were hardly detectable in the naïve state, showed increased expression within juxtaparanodes and paranodes following injury, both in rats and humans.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry and Western blot data in Figures 1 and 8.

claim: Kv1.4 and 1.6 showed increased expression within juxtaparanodes and paranodes following injury in humans.
source: In contrast Kv1.4 and 1.6, which were hardly detectable in the naïve state, showed increased expression within juxtaparanodes and paranodes following injury, both in rats and humans.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry and Western blot data in Figure 7.

claim: Within the dorsal root (a site remote from injury) there was a redistribution of Kv1-channels towards the paranode.
source: Within the dorsal root (a site remote from injury) we noted a redistribution of Kv1-channels towards the paranode.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 8.

claim: Blockade of Kv1 channels with α-DTX after injury reinstated hyperexcitability of A-fibre axons.
source: Blockade of Kv1 channels with α-DTX after injury reinstated hyperexcitability of A-fibre axons and enhanced mechanosensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9.

claim: Blockade of Kv1 channels with α-DTX after injury enhanced mechanosensitivity.
source: Blockade of Kv1 channels with α-DTX after injury reinstated hyperexcitability of A-fibre axons and enhanced mechanosensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological and behavioral data in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Changes in the molecular composition and distribution of axonal Kv1 channels represents a protective mechanism to suppress the hyperexcitability of myelinated sensory axons that follows nerve injury.
source: Changes in the molecular composition and distribution of axonal Kv1 channels, therefore represents a protective mechanism to suppress the hyperexcitability of myelinated sensory axons that follows nerve injury.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, inferred from the combined data showing altered Kv1 channel expression/distribution and the effects of blocking these channels.

claim: Following traumatic nerve injury spontaneous activity develops initially in myelinated and subsequently in unmyelinated sensory axons.
source: Following traumatic nerve injury spontaneous activity develops initially in myelinated and subsequently in unmyelinated sensory axons (Wall and Gutnick, 1974; Kajander and Bennett, 1992; Boucher et al., 2000; Michaelis et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2000a).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The onset of spontaneous activity is associated with the emergence of pain-related sensory changes in animal models.
source: The onset of this spontaneous activity is associated with the emergence of pain-related sensory changes in animal models and is critical for the maintenance of peripheral neuropathic pain (Haroutounian et al., 2014) in patients where selective blockade suggests the involvement of myelinated axons (Campbell et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Spontaneous activity is critical for the maintenance of peripheral neuropathic pain in patients.
source: The onset of this spontaneous activity is associated with the emergence of pain-related sensory changes in animal models and is critical for the maintenance of peripheral neuropathic pain (Haroutounian et al., 2014) in patients where selective blockade suggests the involvement of myelinated axons (Campbell et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Selective blockade in patients suggests the involvement of myelinated axons in neuropathic pain.
source: The onset of this spontaneous activity is associated with the emergence of pain-related sensory changes in animal models and is critical for the maintenance of peripheral neuropathic pain (Haroutounian et al., 2014) in patients where selective blockade suggests the involvement of myelinated axons (Campbell et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ectopic activity is particularly prominent in myelinated afferents.
source: Ectopic activity is particularly prominent in myelinated afferents and peaks within the first few days post injury and then declines over subsequent weeks (Kajander and Bennett, 1992; Liu et al., 2000a; 2000b; Han et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ectopic activity peaks within the first few days post injury and then declines over subsequent weeks.
source: Ectopic activity is particularly prominent in myelinated afferents and peaks within the first few days post injury and then declines over subsequent weeks (Kajander and Bennett, 1992; Liu et al., 2000a; 2000b; Han et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ectopic activity arises both at the neuroma site and at the level of the dorsal root ganglion (DRG).
source: Such ectopic activity arises both at the neuroma site and also at the level of the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) (Han et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2000b; Amir et al., 1999; 2005; Wall and Devor, 1983).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Altered expression, function and trafficking of voltage-gated ion channels are key determinants of excitability changes following nerve injury.
source: Altered expression, function and trafficking of voltage-gated ion channels are key determinants of these excitability changes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Shaker type voltage-gated potassium channels (Kv1 channels) are important determinants of neuronal excitability.
source: Shaker type voltage-gated potassium channels (Kv1 channels) are important determinants of neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Kv1 channels are formed by heteromultimers of α and β subunits.
source: They are formed by heteromultimers of α and β subunits (MacKinnon, 1991).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The characteristics of the outward currents carried by Kv1 channels depend on subunit composition.
source: The characteristics of the outward currents they carry depend on subunit composition.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Sensory neurons are known to express Kv1 channels.
source: Sensory neurons are known to express Kv1 channels and functionally these channels have been shown to limit excitability of sensory neurons
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Kv1.2 suppresses excitability at the level of the sensory neuron cell body.
source: For instance Kv1.2 suppresses excitability at the level of the sensory neuron cell body (Gold et al., 1996; Rasband et al., 2001; Zhao et al., 2013; Everill et al., 1998)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Kv1.1 acts as a 'brake' on mechanosensitivity at the terminals of C-mechano-nociceptor and Aβ-mechanoreceptors.
source: and Kv1.1 acts as a 'brake' on mechanosensitivity at the terminals of C-mechano-nociceptor and Aβ-mechanoreceptors (Hao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Kv1 channels act as excitability brakes for cold thermal sensitivity in intact and damaged axons of primary sensory neurons.
source: Kv1 channels also act as excitability brakes for cold thermal sensitivity in intact and damaged axons of primary sensory neurons (many of such fibres are also mechano-sensitive) (Roza et al., 2006; Madrid et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Kv1 channels are known to be expressed in the juxtaparanodal region of myelinated sensory axons.
source: Kv1 channels are known to be expressed in the juxtaparanodal region of myelinated sensory axons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The distribution of Kv1 channels under pathological neuropathic states is an unexplored issue.
source: An unexplored issue, however, is whether the distribution of these channels changes under pathological neuropathic states.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres depends on the molecular organization of channel domains within the axon.
source: Saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres depends on the molecular organization of channel domains within the axon (Chang and Rasband, 2013)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) are clustered at the node of Ranvier.
source: voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) are clustered at the node of Ranvier.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Nodes are flanked by the paranode, which is an important point of attachment between the axon and the terminal loops of the Schwann cell.
source: Nodes are flanked by the paranode, which is an important point of attachment between the axon and the terminal loops of the Schwann cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Just inside the innermost axoglial junction of the paranode is the juxtaparanode, a domain enriched in Kv1 channels Kv1.1 and 1.2.
source: Just inside the innermost axoglial junction of the paranode is the juxtaparanode a domain enriched in Kv1 channels Kv1.1 and 1.2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The localisation of Kv1.1 and 1.2 to the juxtaparanode is dependent on the formation of a molecular scaffold, which includes the adhesion molecules caspr2 and TAG-1.
source: The localisation of Kv1.1 and 1.2 to the juxtaparanode is dependent on the formation of a molecular scaffold, which includes the adhesion molecules caspr2 and TAG-1 (Poliak et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In the naïve state in adulthood, the juxtaparanodal Kv1 channels are thought not to have a major influence on axon conduction properties of peripheral myelinated axons.
source: In the naïve state in adulthood, the juxtaparanodal Kv1 channels are thought not to have a major influence on axon conduction properties of peripheral myelinated axons (Poliak et al., 2003; Chiu and Ritchie, 1980; Sherratt et al., 1980; Rasband et al., 1998), probably because they are electrically insulated from the node of Ranvier under the myelin sheath.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Juxtaparanodal Kv1 channels are probably electrically insulated from the node of Ranvier under the myelin sheath.
source: In the naïve state in adulthood, the juxtaparanodal Kv1 channels are thought not to have a major influence on axon conduction properties of peripheral myelinated axons (Poliak et al., 2003; Chiu and Ritchie, 1980; Sherratt et al., 1980; Rasband et al., 1998), probably because they are electrically insulated from the node of Ranvier under the myelin sheath.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on established knowledge.

claim: During development Kv1.1 and 1.2 become more widely distributed to include the paranode and even the node.
source: However during development (Vabnick et al., 1999) and following primary demyelination (Rasband et al., 1998) (during which myelin is removed but the axon remains intact), Kv1.1 and 1.2 become more widely distributed to include the paranode and even the node (Arroyo et al., 2004), and can act to suppress excitability.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Following primary demyelination Kv1.1 and 1.2 become more widely distributed to include the paranode and even the node.
source: However during development (Vabnick et al., 1999) and following primary demyelination (Rasband et al., 1998) (during which myelin is removed but the axon remains intact), Kv1.1 and 1.2 become more widely distributed to include the paranode and even the node (Arroyo et al., 2004), and can act to suppress excitability.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Kv1.1 and 1.2 can act to suppress excitability when they become more widely distributed during development and following primary demyelination.
source: However during development (Vabnick et al., 1999) and following primary demyelination (Rasband et al., 1998) (during which myelin is removed but the axon remains intact), Kv1.1 and 1.2 become more widely distributed to include the paranode and even the node (Arroyo et al., 2004), and can act to suppress excitability.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Kv1.1 and 1.2 expression within the soma is known to be down-regulated following axon transection.
source: Although Kv1.1 and 1.2 expression within the soma is known to be down-regulated following axon transection, and this leads to hyperexcitability at the soma (Rasband et al., 1998; Ishikawa et al., 1999; Park et al., 2003), the distribution of these channels at the nodal complex and damaged nerve terminal (in the neuroma that forms) has not been examined.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Down-regulation of Kv1.1 and 1.2 expression within the soma following axon transection leads to hyperexcitability at the soma.
source: Although Kv1.1 and 1.2 expression within the soma is known to be down-regulated following axon transection, and this leads to hyperexcitability at the soma (Rasband et al., 1998; Ishikawa et al., 1999; Park et al., 2003), the distribution of these channels at the nodal complex and damaged nerve terminal (in the neuroma that forms) has not been examined.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The distribution of Kv1.1 and 1.2 at the nodal complex and damaged nerve terminal (in the neuroma that forms) has not been examined.
source: Although Kv1.1 and 1.2 expression within the soma is known to be down-regulated following axon transection, and this leads to hyperexcitability at the soma (Rasband et al., 1998; Ishikawa et al., 1999; Park et al., 2003), the distribution of these channels at the nodal complex and damaged nerve terminal (in the neuroma that forms) has not been examined.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Little is known regarding the distribution of other members of the shaker type Kv1 channels family such as Kv1.4 and 1.6 following nerve injury.
source: Furthermore, little is known regarding the distribution of other members of the shaker type Kv1 channels family such as Kv1.4 and 1.6 following nerve injury.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Within a neuroma, expression levels of Kv1.1 and 1.2 are markedly reduced.
source: Here we show that within a neuroma, expression levels of Kv1.1 and 1.2 are markedly reduced but over time Kv1.4 and 1.6 expression increases within juxtaparanodes and paranodes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Over time Kv1.4 and 1.6 expression increases within juxtaparanodes and paranodes in the neuroma.
source: Here we show that within a neuroma, expression levels of Kv1.1 and 1.2 are markedly reduced but over time Kv1.4 and 1.6 expression increases within juxtaparanodes and paranodes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: At sites remote from injury, there is a gradual redistribution of Kv1 channels to the paranode.
source: At sites remote from injury, there is also a gradual redistribution of Kv1 channels to the paranode.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Changes in subunit expression and redistribution of Kv1 channels act as a 'brake' on the hyperexcitable state that arises in myelinated axons following traumatic nerve injury.
source: Electrophysiological and behavioural experiments suggest that changes in subunit expression and redistribution of Kv1 channels act a 'brake' on the hyperexcitable state that arises in myelinated axons following traumatic nerve injury.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the introduction, inferred from electrophysiological and behavioral data in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: Over 90% of the nodes in naïve axons presented a characteristic morphology with Nav clustering in the centre, surrounded by caspr at both sides and Kv1.2 clustered within the juxtaparanode.
source: In the naïve axon, we observed that over 90% (mean 91 ± SEM 2.9%, n = 4 animals) of the nodes presented a characteristic morphology with Nav clustering in the centre, surrounded by caspr at both sides and Kv1.2 clustered within the juxtaparanode.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: Kv1.4 and 1.6 are expressed by DRG cells.
source: Of other members of the Kv1 channels family, Kv1.4 and 1.6 are expressed by DRG cells (Everill et al., 1998; Thakur et al., 2014; Chiu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the naïve state Kv1.4 was only expressed within a very small proportion of nodes (5.5 ± 4.6%, n = 4 animals) within the juxtaparanode.
source: We found that in the naïve state Kv1.4 was only expressed within a very small proportion of nodes (5.5 ± 4.6%, n = 4 animals) within the juxtaparanode and Kv1.6 was not present within the nodal complex (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Kv1.6 was not present within the nodal complex in the naïve state.
source: We found that in the naïve state Kv1.4 was only expressed within a very small proportion of nodes (5.5 ± 4.6%, n = 4 animals) within the juxtaparanode and Kv1.6 was not present within the nodal complex (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: At the site of the neuroma (day 7 and 21), only half of the nodes demonstrated typical morphology.
source: At the site of the neuroma (day 7 and 21), only half of the nodes demonstrated this typical morphology (day 7 = 47.5 ± 5.1%, day 21 = 46 ± 6.%, n = 4 animals per group, 36–64 nodes per animal)
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: At day 7 after injury, Kv1.2 channels were not located strictly in the juxtaparanodal regions but also overlapped with paranodal proteins.
source: At day 7 after injury, Kv1.2 channels were not located strictly not only in the juxtaparanodal regions but also overlapped with paranodal proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: In naïve axons the distance between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr was 3.8 ± 0.2 μm.
source: In naïve axons the distance between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr was 3.8 ± 0.2 μm, and the distance between Nav channels staining and the start of Kv1.2 staining was 4.2 ± 0.2 μm, resulting in a relatively small, albeit positive, difference between these distances (0.5 ± 0.08 μm, n = 4 animals, 25–40 nodes per animal), indicating there was no overlap.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: At day 7 after injury, the distance between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr was 4 ± 0.1 μm, and the distance between Nav channels staining and the start of Kv1.2 staining was 3.2 ± 0.2 μm, giving a negative value for the difference between both distances (-0.8 ± 0.1 μm, n = 3 animals, 32–35 nodes per animal), which indicates that the Kv1 channels were co-localised with caspr staining and moving closer to the node.
source: At day 7 after injury, the distance between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr was 4 ± 0.1 μm, and the distance between Nav channels staining and the start of Kv1.2 staining was 3.2 ± 0.2 μm, giving a negative value for the difference between both distances (-0.8 ± 0.1 μm, n = 3 animals, 32–35 nodes per animal), which indicates that the Kv1 channels were co-localised with caspr staining and moving closer to the node (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The distance between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr staining remained unchanged after injury.
source: Note that the distance between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr staining remained unchanged after injury, while the distance between Nav channels staining and the start of Kv1.2 staining was significantly reduced.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: The distance between Nav channels staining and the start of Kv1.2 staining was significantly reduced after injury.
source: Note that the distance between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr staining remained unchanged after injury, while the distance between Nav channels staining and the start of Kv1.2 staining was significantly reduced.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: Contactin-associated protein-like 2 (Caspr2) forms a complex with Kv1 channels at the juxtaparanode.
source: Contactin-associated protein-like 2 (Caspr2) forms a complex with Kv1 channels at the juxtaparanode (Chiu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: At day 7 after injury, caspr2 co-localised with caspr staining and had moved closer to the node together with Kv1 channels.
source: At day 7 after injury, the distance between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr was 4.1 ± 0.2 μm, and the distance between Nav channels staining and the start of caspr2 staining was 2.8 ± 0.2 μm, giving a negative value for the difference between both distances (-1.2 ± 0.1 μm, n = 3 animals, 30 nodes per animal), which indicates that the caspr2 co-localised with caspr staining and had moved closer to the node together with Kv1 channels (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The effect on Kv1.2 re-localization remains the same at the site far from the neuroma (1 cm proximal).
source: The effect on Kv12 re-localization remains the same at the site far from the neuroma: The difference between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr distance and Nav channels staining and the start of Kv1.2 distance was -1 ± 0.09 μm, at the site close to the neuroma and -1.1 ± 0.09 μm, at the site far from the neuroma (p = 0.6, n = 5 animals, 24–26 nodes per animal).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: The effect on caspr2 re-localization is slightly smaller at the site 1cm proximal to the neuroma compared with the site close to the neuroma, but it is still significantly different from the naïve.
source: The effect on caspr2 re-localization is slightly smaller at the site 1cm proximal to the neuroma compared with the site close to the neuroma, but it is still significantly different from the naïve (p<0.001): The difference between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr distance and Nav channels staining and the start of caspr2 distance was -1 ± 0.1 μm, at the site close to the neuroma and -0.5 ± 0.1 μm, at the site far from the neuroma (p = 0.06, n = 5 animals, 21–26 nodes per animal, Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The axo-glial distance was not significantly changed between sham-operated and neuroma animals (sham = 9.7 ± 0.4 nm, neuroma = 11.4 ± 0.7 nm, n = 4–5 animals per group, 6–9 nodes per animal one way ANOVA p = 0.08).
source: The close apposition between the axon and the paranodal loop was unchanged as the axo-glial distance was not significantly changed (sham = 9.7 ± 0.4 nm, neuroma = 11.4 ± 0.7 nm, n = 4–5 animals per group, 6–9 nodes per animal one way ANOVA p = 0.08).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electron microscopy analysis.

claim: There was a small but significant increase in the maximal distance between loops (sham = 12.5 ± 1 nm, neuroma = 18.9 ± 1.4 nm, one way ANOVA, p = 0.005).
source: We observed a small but significant increase in the maximal distance between loops (sham = 12.5 ± 1 nm, neuroma = 18.9 ± 1.4 nm, one way ANOVA, p = 0.005).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Although there was no major disruption of the septate axoglial junctions there was a small but significant increased separation between the paranodal loops.
source: In summary, these results suggest that although there was no major disruption of the septate axoglial junctions there was a small but significant increased separation between the paranodal loops (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The axonal diameter at the node did not change.
source: Note that the axonal diameter at the node did not change (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: βII spectrin is a cytoskeletal protein that has recently been shown to be essential for the localization of Kv1 channels to the juxtaparanode.
source: βII spectrin is a cytoskeletal protein that has recently been shown to be essential for the localization of Kv1 channels to the juxtaparanode and is proposed to form a sub-membranous barrier to lateral diffusion of Kv1 channels into the paranode (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: βII spectrin is proposed to form a sub-membranous barrier to lateral diffusion of Kv1 channels into the paranode.
source: βII spectrin is a cytoskeletal protein that has recently been shown to be essential for the localization of Kv1 channels to the juxtaparanode and is proposed to form a sub-membranous barrier to lateral diffusion of Kv1 channels into the paranode (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: βII spectrin is expressed at the paranode and juxtaparanode in the neuroma.
source: Using IHC, we looked at βII spectrin in the neuroma and found that it is expressed at the paranode and juxtaparanode.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: The expression of βII spectrin at the paranodal domain was reduced by more than half compared to naive (immunofluorescence normalised to naïve: 0.4 ± 0.02, p<0.001, t-test, n = 50–83 heminodes).
source: We quantified the staining at the paranodal domain and found that the expression of this protein was reduced by more than half compared to naive (immunofluorescence normalised to naïve: 0.4 ± 0.02, p<0.001, t-test, n = 50–83 heminodes, a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: βII spectrin expression in the DRG was reduced by 30% following nerve injury compared to naive (expression relative to naïve: 0.7 ± 0.08, p = 0.04, t-test, n = 4).
source: To further quantify the change of expression of this protein in the neuron, we performed Western blotting in the soma of sensory neurons (dorsal root ganglia- DRG) and observed a 30% decrease following nerve injury compared to naive (expression relative to naïve: 0.7 ± 0.08, p = 0.04, t-test, n = 4, Figure 5c–d).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: At day 21 after injury, very few of the nodes at the neuroma site showed Kv1.2 immunostaining (8.3 ± 0.8% in neuroma vs. 86.1 ± 4.4% in naive, n = 4 animals per group, 25 nodes per animal p<0.001 t-test).
source: At day 21 after injury, in marked contrast with the naïve axons, very few of the nodes at the neuroma site (day 21) showed Kv1.2 immunostaining (8.3 ± 0.8% in neuroma vs. 86.1 ± 4.4% in naive, n = 4 animals per group, 25 nodes per animal p<0.001 t-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: Most of the nodes at the neuroma site (day 21) showed intense Kv1.4 immunostaining (73.3 ± 12% in injured vs. 5.5 ± 4 in naive, n = 4 animals per group, 30 nodes per animal p<0.001 t-test).
source: Conversely, most of the nodes at the neuroma site (day 21) showed intense Kv1.4 immunostaining (73.3 ± 12% in injured vs. 5.5 ± 4 in naive, n = 4 animals per group, 30 nodes per animal p<0.001 t-test) and Kv1.6 immunostaining (66.6 ± 14% vs. in injured vs. none in naive, n= 4 animals per group, 30 nodes per animal p<0.001 t-test) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Most of the nodes at the neuroma site (day 21) showed Kv1.6 immunostaining (66.6 ± 14% vs. in injured vs. none in naive, n= 4 animals per group, 30 nodes per animal p<0.001 t-test).
source: Conversely, most of the nodes at the neuroma site (day 21) showed intense Kv1.4 immunostaining (73.3 ± 12% in injured vs. 5.5 ± 4 in naive, n = 4 animals per group, 30 nodes per animal p<0.001 t-test) and Kv1.6 immunostaining (66.6 ± 14% vs. in injured vs. none in naive, n= 4 animals per group, 30 nodes per animal p<0.001 t-test) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 expression were significantly reduced at days 7 and 21 following nerve injury.
source: We used Western blotting to quantify the expression of the different α subunits and found that Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 expression were significantly reduced at days 7 and 21 following nerve injury, while Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 were significantly upregulated at the neuroma site (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 were significantly upregulated at the neuroma site at days 7 and 21 following nerve injury.
source: We used Western blotting to quantify the expression of the different α subunits and found that Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 expression were significantly reduced at days 7 and 21 following nerve injury, while Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 were significantly upregulated at the neuroma site (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Kv1.2 expression is reduced in the DRG after injury.
source: We looked at Kv1 channel expression in the DRG using IHC and we observed that Kv1.2 expression is reduced after injury, while Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 expression remains unchanged (Figure 6a)
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 expression remains unchanged in the DRG after injury.
source: We looked at Kv1 channel expression in the DRG using IHC and we observed that Kv1.2 expression is reduced after injury, while Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 expression remains unchanged (Figure 6a)
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The expression of Kv1.2 within the DRG was significantly reduced following nerve injury.
source: The expression of Kv1.2 was significantly reduced following nerve injury (Figure 6b–e) consistent with previous findings, (Everill et al., 1998; Ishikawa et al., 1999; Kim et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2004)
evidence: This is a primary finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6, consistent with previous literature.

claim: There was a trend for a reduction in Kv1.1 in the DRG following nerve injury although this did not reach significance.
source: and there was a trend for a reduction in Kv1.1 although this did not reach significance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Western blot analysis.

claim: The expression of Kv1.4 and 1.6 within the DRG did not significantly change following injury.
source: The expression of Kv1.4 and 1.6 within the DRG did not significantly change following injury (one Way ANOVA, n = 6 per group) suggesting that increased expression within the juxtaparanode and paranode at the neuroma site is a likely consequence of altered trafficking of these proteins rather than global changes in expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Increased expression of Kv1.4 and 1.6 within the juxtaparanode and paranode at the neuroma site is a likely consequence of altered trafficking of these proteins rather than global changes in expression.
source: The expression of Kv1.4 and 1.6 within the DRG did not significantly change following injury (one Way ANOVA, n = 6 per group) suggesting that increased expression within the juxtaparanode and paranode at the neuroma site is a likely consequence of altered trafficking of these proteins rather than global changes in expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that DRG expression does not change while axonal expression increases.

claim: Only Kv1.2 is expressed in the juxtaparanode of healthy human subjects (90 ± 10% of nodes were Kv1.2 positive).
source: IHC (n = 3 per group, 8–10 nodes per patient) showed that only Kv1.2 is expressed in the juxtaparanode of healthy subjects (90 ± 10% of nodes were Kv1.2 positive) with absent Kv1.4 and 1.6 staining as observed in the rat.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis of human tissue.

claim: Kv1.4 and 1.6 staining is absent in the juxtaparanode of healthy human subjects.
source: IHC (n = 3 per group, 8–10 nodes per patient) showed that only Kv1.2 is expressed in the juxtaparanode of healthy subjects (90 ± 10% of nodes were Kv1.2 positive) with absent Kv1.4 and 1.6 staining as observed in the rat.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis of human tissue.

claim: In human neuroma Kv1.2 expression in the juxtaparanode was minimal (13.3 ± 8.1%).
source: However, in neuroma Kv1.2 expression in the juxtaparanode was minimal (13.3 ± 8.1%) whilst Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 were expressed in most of the nodes (92.5 ± 7.4% for Kv1.4; 73.5 ± 8.8 for Kv1.6) (Figure 7a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis of human tissue shown in Figure 7.

claim: In human neuroma Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 were expressed in most of the nodes (92.5 ± 7.4% for Kv1.4; 73.5 ± 8.8 for Kv1.6).
source: However, in neuroma Kv1.2 expression in the juxtaparanode was minimal (13.3 ± 8.1%) whilst Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 were expressed in most of the nodes (92.5 ± 7.4% for Kv1.4; 73.5 ± 8.8 for Kv1.6) (Figure 7a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis of human tissue shown in Figure 7.

claim: Kv1.2 expression was significantly decreased in human neuroma compared to control nerve (to 0.48 ± 0.1 of the control, Mann-Whitney U-Test, p 0.005).
source: We used western blotting to quantify Kv1 channels proteins in the nerves of the patients (n = 6 per group) and found that Kv1.2 expression was significantly decreased in neuroma compared to control nerve (to 0.48 ± 0.1 of the control, Mann-Whitney U-Test, p 0.005).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Western blot analysis of human tissue shown in Figure 7.

claim: Expression of Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 were significantly increased in human neuroma compared to controls (to 6.3 ± 3.5, and 9.4 ± 6.6 of the control respectively, Mann-Whitney U-Test p = 0.005 both).
source: In contrast, expression of Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 were significantly increased in neuroma compared to controls (to 6.3 ± 3.5, and 9.4 ± 6.6 of the control respectively, Mann-Whitney U-Test p = 0.005 both) (Figure 7c–d).
evidence: This is a primary finding from Western blot analysis of human tissue shown in Figure 7.

claim: In the dorsal roots from naïve animals, there was no overlap between Kv1.2 and caspr staining (difference between distances: 0.5 ± 0.1 μm, n = 4 animals, 25–32 nodes per animal).
source: In the dorsal roots from naïve animals, the distance between Nav channels staining and the end of caspr was 3.5 ± 0.2 μm, and the distance between Nav channels staining and the start of Kv1.2 staining was 4 ± 0.2 μm, resulting in a small positive difference between these distances (0.5 ± 0.1 μm, n = 4 animals, 25–32 nodes per animal), indicating there was no overlap.
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: Seven days after transection of L5 spinal nerve the distance between Kv1.2 and caspr was still positive (0.24 ± 0.05 μm, n = 4 animals).
source: Seven days after transection of L5 spinal nerve this distance was still positive (0.24 ± 0.05 μm, n = 4 animals; distance Nav-end caspr 3.7 ± 0.2 μm, distance Nav-start Kv1.2 3.9 ± 0.1 μm; 30–40 nodes per animal).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: At 21 days after nerve injury, there was a significant overlap between the end of caspr staining and the start of the Kv1.2 staining in the dorsal root (-1.4 ± 0.3 μm, n = 4 animals, 38–40 nodes per animal, one way ANOVA, p<0.001).
source: However, at 21 days after nerve injury, we noted a significant overlap between the end of caspr staining and the start of the Kv1.2 staining (-1.4 ± 0.3 μm, n = 4 animals, 38–40 nodes per animal, one way ANOVA, p<0.001; distance between Nav-end caspr 3.9 ± 0.4 μm, distance between Nav-start Kv1.2 2.5 ± 0.4 μm).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Kv1.2 is still clearly present after nerve injury within the dorsal root in contrast to the neuroma site.
source: We observed this novel localisation of Kv1.2 in the paranode which (in contrast to the neuroma site) is still clearly present after nerve injury within the dorsal root.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: Novel expression of Kv1.4 and 1.6 was observed in the dorsal root of injured animals, and these were localised to the paranode in addition to the juxtaparanode.
source: We also observed novel expression of Kv1.4 and 1.6 in the dorsal root of injured animals, and these were localised to the paranode in addition to the juxtaparanode (the distance between end of caspr and start of Kv1.4 and 1.6 staining was -1.7 ± 0.6 μm and -1.07 ± 0.2 μm respectively; for Kv1.4 distance between Nav-end caspr 3.6 ± 0.4 μm, distance between Nav-start Kv1.4 1.9 ± 0.6 μm; for Kv1.6: distance between Nav-end caspr 3.4 ± 0.4 μm, distance between Nav-start Kv1.6 1.6 ± 0.4 μm n = 4 animals per group, 30–35 nodes per animal Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Caspr2 is mobilized into the paranode regions in a similar way to Kv1 channels in the dorsal root after injury.
source: Interestingly, we observed that caspr2 is mobilized into the paranode regions in a similar way to Kv1 channels; the difference between the Nav-caspr staining distance and the Nav-caspr2 distance is minimal in naïve roots (0.5 ± 0.1 μm; distance between Nav-end caspr 3.8 ± 0.3 μm, distance between Nav-start caspr2 4.3 ± 0.4 μm, 30–38 nodes per animal 4 animals), and after SNT, this distance becomes negative (-0.88 ± 0.1 μm, n = 5 animals; distance between Nav-end caspr 3.4 ± 0.3 μm, distance between Nav-start caspr2 2.5 ± 0.3 μm 35–40 nodes per animal p<0.001, t-test) indicating an overlap between caspr and caspr2 immuno-labeling (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding from quantitative immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Spontaneous activity in naïve axons was present in less than 5% of A-fibres (4.5%).
source: Spontaneous activity in naïve axons was present in less than 5% of A-fibres (4.5%).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: In the naïve situation, the incidence of spontaneous activity did not significantly change after α-DTX (5.4 and 9.8% of myelinated afferents when the toxin was applied to nerve stump or L5 DRG, respectively).
source: In the naïve situation (n = 222 neurons, 10 animals, Figure 9a), the incidence of spontaneous activity did not significantly change after α-DTX (5.4 and 9.8% of myelinated afferents when the toxin was applied to nerve stump or L5 DRG, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 9.

claim: Two days after transecting the sciatic nerve, spontaneous activity at the injured nerve increased to 22% of myelinated afferents.
source: Two days after transecting the sciatic nerve (n = 291 neurons, 4 animals), spontaneous activity at the injured nerve increased to 22% of myelinated afferents, and it was similar with or without toxin (toxin applied to neuroma 26.1%, toxin applied to the L5 DRG 26%).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: At 7 days after nerve injury the proportion of spontaneously active afferents had decreased to 6.2%.
source: However, at 7 days after nerve injury (n = 241 neurons, 7 animals) the proportion of spontaneously active afferents had decreased to 6.2%, and application of the toxin now induced a significant increase in proportion of spontaneously firing myelinated afferents (11.2% toxin at the neuroma p = 0.07, and 15.6% toxin to L5 DRG, p = 0.002, chi-square test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 9.

claim: At 7 days after nerve injury, application of α-DTX induced a significant increase in proportion of spontaneously firing myelinated afferents (11.2% toxin at the neuroma p = 0.07, and 15.6% toxin to L5 DRG, p = 0.002).
source: However, at 7 days after nerve injury (n = 241 neurons, 7 animals) the proportion of spontaneously active afferents had decreased to 6.2%, and application of the toxin now induced a significant increase in proportion of spontaneously firing myelinated afferents (11.2% toxin at the neuroma p = 0.07, and 15.6% toxin to L5 DRG, p = 0.002, chi-square test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 9.

claim: At day 21 after injury spontaneous activity has decreased to baseline levels (2.5% of afferents within the dorsal root).
source: At day 21 after injury (n = 237 neurons, 7 animals) spontaneous activity has decreased to baseline levels (2.5% of afferents within the dorsal root), but application of the toxin to both neuroma site or L5 DRG significantly increased the proportion of myelinated afferents demonstrating spontaneous activity (7.2% p = 0.03 and 17.7 ±% p<0.001 respectively, chi-square test) (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 9.

claim: At day 21 after injury, application of α-DTX to both neuroma site or L5 DRG significantly increased the proportion of myelinated afferents demonstrating spontaneous activity (7.2% p = 0.03 and 17.7 ±% p<0.001 respectively).
source: At day 21 after injury (n = 237 neurons, 7 animals) spontaneous activity has decreased to baseline levels (2.5% of afferents within the dorsal root), but application of the toxin to both neuroma site or L5 DRG significantly increased the proportion of myelinated afferents demonstrating spontaneous activity (7.2% p = 0.03 and 17.7 ±% p<0.001 respectively, chi-square test) (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 9.

claim: Kv1 channels appear to have a role in the recovery from increased excitability following nerve injury.
source: In summary, we observed an acute increase in spontaneous activity following nerve injury, which was reversed with time. However, at this later time, blockade of Kv1 channels (which had no effect in the naïve state) could reinstate spontaneous activity almost to levels seen acutely after nerve injury. Therefore, Kv1 channels appear to have a role in the recovery from increased excitability following nerve injury (Figure 9b–d).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the electrophysiological data showing that blocking Kv1 channels reinstates hyperexcitability.

claim: In the presence of α-DTX, significantly more neurons respond to mechanical stimulation at the neuroma site using a 15 g von Frey filament (with 15 g: pre 24.7%, post 30.5%, p = 0.006, chi-square test; n = 259 neurons).
source: In the presence of α-DTX, significantly more neurons responded to mechanical stimulation using a 15g von Frey filament at the neuroma site at day 21 (with 4 g: pre 17.9% post 21.8%; with 8 g: pre 22.1% post 26%; with 15 g: pre 24.7%, post 30.5%, p = 0.006, chi-square test; n = 259 neurons; Figure 9e–f).
evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 9.

claim: At baseline, the withdrawal threshold was high and did not change with the application of α DTX (vehicle: 142.9 ± 13 g, toxin 150 ± 17.7 g, n = 9 animals per group).
source: At baseline, the withdrawal threshold was high and did not change with the application of α DTX (vehicle: 142.9 ± 13 g, toxin 150 ± 17.7 g, n = 9 animals per group).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral testing shown in Figure 10.

claim: Three days after injury, the withdrawal threshold dropped to 8.2 ± 0.6 g and was not changed by applying the toxin (9.7 ± 1.1 g).
source: Three days after injury, this threshold dropped to 8.2 ± 0.6 g and was not changed by applying the toxin (9.7 ± 1.1 g) (n = 9 animals per group).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral testing shown in Figure 10.

claim: With time the withdrawal threshold began to normalise reaching 12.9 ± 0.6 g at 7 days and 44.8 ± 1.6 g at 21 days.
source: However, with time this threshold began to normalise reaching 12.9 ± 0.6 g at 7 days (n = 8) and 44.8 ± 1.6 g at 21 days (n = 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral testing shown in Figure 10.

claim: When αDTX was injected, the recovery of withdrawal threshold was not seen and thresholds stayed low (day 7: 6.9 ± 0.9 g, p = 0.003, n = 9; day 21: 13 ± 2.1 g, p<0.001, n = 7).
source: When we injected αDTX, this recovery was not seen and thresholds stayed low (day 7: 6.9 ± 0.9 g, p = 0.003, n = 9; day 21: 13 ± 2.1 g, p<0.001, n = 7, RM two way ANOVA Figure 10).
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral testing shown in Figure 10.

claim: α-DTX is a selective blocker for Kv1.1, Kv1.2 and Kv1.6 but has little activity against Kv1.4.
source: The time point when the mechanical hypersensitivity began to recover in injured animals coincides with the time when Kv1.1 and Kv1.2 are reduced but Kv1.4 and Kv1.6 are being expressed. α-DTX is a selective blocker for Kv1.1, Kv1.2 and Kv1.6 but has little activity against Kv1.4.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the pharmacology of α-DTX.

claim: CP 339818 hydrochloride is a selective blocker of Kv1.3 and Kv1.4.
source: CP 339818 hydrochloride however, which is a selective blocker of Kv1.3 and Kv1.4 (Nguyen et al., 1996), did not have any effect on mechanical hypersensitivity at early or late time-points post injury
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: CP 339818 hydrochloride did not have any effect on mechanical hypersensitivity at early or late time-points post injury.
source: CP 339818 hydrochloride however, which is a selective blocker of Kv1.3 and Kv1.4 (Nguyen et al., 1996), did not have any effect on mechanical hypersensitivity at early or late time-points post injury suggesting that Kv1.4 is dispensable for the suppression of hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is a primary finding from behavioral testing.

claim: Kv1.4 is dispensable for the suppression of hyperexcitability.
source: CP 339818 hydrochloride however, which is a selective blocker of Kv1.3 and Kv1.4 (Nguyen et al., 1996), did not have any effect on mechanical hypersensitivity at early or late time-points post injury suggesting that Kv1.4 is dispensable for the suppression of hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of CP 339818 hydrochloride on mechanical hypersensitivity.

claim: Following traumatic nerve injury there is an initial inflammatory response, demyelination and axonal die-back within the proximal nerve stump.
source: Following traumatic nerve injury there is an initial inflammatory response, demyelination and axonal die-back within the proximal nerve stump.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Axonal die-back is followed by axonal sprouting which is often misdirected.
source: This is followed by axonal sprouting (Fried and Devor, 1988; DeFelipe, 1991) (which is often misdirected) as well as proliferation of connective tissue and glial cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nerve injury can lead to a region of nerve swelling, a neuroma, the development of which is well documented in patients.
source: This can lead to a region of nerve swelling, a neuroma, the development of which is well documented in patients (Scadding, 1981; DeFelipe, 1991; Young, 1942).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nerve injury is often associated with ongoing pain, dysaesthesia and evoked pain.
source: Nerve injury is often associated with ongoing pain, dysaesthesia and evoked pain; many patients report that touching the skin overlying or compression of the neuroma site can elicit pain and dysaesthesia (Nikolajsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Many patients report that touching the skin overlying or compression of the neuroma site can elicit pain and dysaesthesia.
source: Nerve injury is often associated with ongoing pain, dysaesthesia and evoked pain; many patients report that touching the skin overlying or compression of the neuroma site can elicit pain and dysaesthesia (Nikolajsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In many patients, the treatment of neuropathic pain remains inadequate.
source: Unfortunately in many patients, the treatment of neuropathic pain remains inadequate (Finnerup et al., 2015) and is associated with significant disability (Stokvis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neuropathic pain is associated with significant disability.
source: Unfortunately in many patients, the treatment of neuropathic pain remains inadequate (Finnerup et al., 2015) and is associated with significant disability (Stokvis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: It has previously been documented that within a neuroma nodes of Ranvier become disorganised.
source: It has previously been documented that within a neuroma nodes of Ranvier become disorganised (Levinson et al., 2012) and we confirm that here with the majority nodes showing abnormalities such as being elongated, split, heminodes or showing Nav in the absence of caspr.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation, and confirmed by the current study.

claim: Voltage-gated sodium channels are known to accumulate particularly within axon tips and on denuded axons of the neuroma.
source: Voltage-gated sodium channels are known to accumulate particularly within axon tips and on denuded axons of the neuroma (England et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Much less is known regarding the distribution of Kv1 channels changes within the neuroma.
source: Much less is known regarding the distribution of Kv1 channels changes within the neuroma.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Increased availability of Kv1 channels within the paranodes and altered subunit composition appears to fulfil an adaptive role in suppressing excessive excitability in myelinated afferents.
source: In conclusion, we have found major changes in Kv1 channels subunit composition and distribution within the axolemma of myelinated axons following traumatic nerve injury. In contrast to the soma in which Kv1 channels expression is reduced this increased availability of Kv1 channels within the paranodes and altered subunit composition appears to fulfil an adaptive role in suppressing excessive excitability in myelinated afferents.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from the combined data.

claim: Within the neuroma new nodes of Ranvier will be formed as a consequence of myelination of new axon sprouts and remyelination of denuded axons.
source: This altered expression and localisation is likely to partially reflect the altered relationship between axons and myelinating Schwann cells. Within the neuroma new nodes of Ranvier will be formed as a consequence of myelination of new axon sprouts and remyelination of denuded axons (Dorsi et al., 2008; Dyck et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During developmental myelination and remyelination following primary demyelination Kv1.1 and 1.2 can at early time points be observed in other regions apart from the juxtaparanode before being restricted to the juxtaparanode as the nodal complex matures.
source: During developmental myelination and remyelination following primary demyelination (in which the axon remains intact) Kv1.1 and 1.2 can at early time points be observed in other regions apart from the juxtaparanode (at the node of Ranvier and the paranode) before being restricted to the juxtaparanode as the nodal complex matures (Rasband et al., 1998; Vabnick et al., 1999; Poliak et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The transverse bands are important points of attachment between the axon and the paranodal loops of the Schwann cell.
source: The transverse bands are important points of attachment between the axon and the paranodal loops of the Schwann cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Axoglial septate-like junctions are formed by the interaction of caspr and contactin on the axolemma binding with the 155Kd isoform of Neurofascin expressed on the Schwann cell paranodal loops.
source: These axoglial septate-like junctions are formed by the interaction of caspr (Bhat et al., 2001) and contactin (Boyle et al., 2001) on the axolemma binding with the 155Kd isoform of Neurofascin expressed on the Schwann cell paranodal loops (Tait et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Axoglial junctions act as diffusion barriers between the nodal and juxtaparanodal membrane.
source: These junctions act as diffusion barriers between the nodal and juxtaparanodal membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Mice lacking caspr have absent transverse bands, increased distance between the axon and Schwann cell membrane, disorganisation of the paranodal loops and Kv1 channels extend into the paranode.
source: Mice lacking caspr (Bhat et al., 2001), contactin (Boyle et al., 2001) or NF155 (Pillai et al., 2009; Sherman et al., 2005) have absent transverse bands, increased distance between the axon and Schwann cell membrane, disorganisation of the paranodal loops and probably as a consequence of the loss of this lateral diffusion barrier Kv1 channels are noted to extend into the paranode.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In mice lacking ceramide galactosyl transferase in which all-putative adhesion components of the paranodal junction are lacking, Kv1.2 and caspr2 are also mis-localised to the paranodes.
source: Similarly in mice lacking ceramide galactosyl transferase in which all-putative adhesion components of the paranodal junction are lacking, Kv1.2 and caspr2 are also mis-localised to the paranodes (Poliak et al., 2001; 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In mice lacking βII spectrin expression in axons Kv1 channels were no longer restricted to the juxtaparanode but could also be observed in the paranode even though the structural integrity of axoglial junctions was intact.
source: A recent publication has demonstrated that in mice lacking βII spectrin expression in axons Kv1 channels were no longer restricted to the juxtaparanode but could also be observed in the paranode even though the structural integrity of axoglial junctions was intact (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: βII spectrin contributes to the sub-membranous cytoskeleton of the axon-linking membrane proteins to actin and appears to act as a barrier limiting the lateral diffusion of membrane proteins.
source: βII spectrin contributes to the sub-membranous cytoskeleton of the axon-linking membrane proteins to actin and appears to act as a barrier limiting the lateral diffusion of membrane proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Paranodal expression of βII spectrin was reduced following axotomy.
source: We found that paranodal expression of βII spectrin was reduced following axotomy and a reduction in this sub-membranous barrier is compatible with the lateral movement of Kv1 channels into this region that we observed.
evidence: This is a primary finding from immunohistochemistry and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: A reduction in βII spectrin sub-membranous barrier is compatible with the lateral movement of Kv1 channels into the paranode.
source: We found that paranodal expression of βII spectrin was reduced following axotomy and a reduction in this sub-membranous barrier is compatible with the lateral movement of Kv1 channels into this region that we observed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in βII spectrin and the known role of this protein as a diffusion barrier.

claim: Caspr2 complexes with and is important for the correct localisation of Kv1 channels.
source: Caspr2 complexes with and is important for the correct localisation of Kv1 channels (Poliak et al., 1999; 2003) suggesting that this whole protein complex is mis-localised following nerve injury.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The whole Kv1 channel-caspr2 protein complex is mis-localised following nerve injury.
source: Caspr2 complexes with and is important for the correct localisation of Kv1 channels (Poliak et al., 1999; 2003) suggesting that this whole protein complex is mis-localised following nerve injury.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both Kv1 channels and caspr2 are mis-localised.

claim: Kv1.2 can undergo phosphorylation, which impacts on surface expression/localisation.
source: Phosphorylation events may have a role to play as Kv1.2 can undergo phosphorylation, which impacts on surface expression/localisation (Gu and Gu, 2011; Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Following axonal injury sensory axons become hyper-excitable and this is important in driving and maintaining neuropathic pain.
source: Following axonal injury sensory axons become hyper-excitable and this is important in driving and maintaining neuropathic pain (Han et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A recent study showed that myelinated sensory fibres are key in maintaining mechanical allodynia in several neuropathic pain models.
source: A recent study showed that myelinated sensory fibres are key in maintaining mechanical allodynia in several neuropathic pain models (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Spontaneous activity and mechanical stimulus evoked activity has been recorded in myelinated afferents innervating neuroma using microneurography.
source: Spontaneous activity and mechanical stimulus evoked activity has been recorded in myelinated afferents innervating neuroma using microneurography (Nyström and Hagbarth, 1981).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The role of Kv1 channels has mainly focussed on their importance in suppressing excitability at the soma rather than the axon following injury.
source: The role of Kv1 channels has mainly focussed on their importance in suppressing excitability at the soma rather than the axon following injury.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The K currents mediated by Kv1 channels are reduced when measured at the soma both in small and large diameter DRG cells following axotomy.
source: Correspondingly, the K currents mediated by such channels are reduced when measured at the soma (Yang et al., 2004) both in small and large diameter DRG cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The expression of Kv1 channels within the DRG soma and the axon should not be assumed to be the same.
source: The expression of Kv1 channels within the DRG soma and the axon should not be assumed to be the same: For instance the expression of Kv1.6 remains stable within the DRG both at the level of mRNA and protein (see Kim et al. (2002), Yang et al. (2004) and our own data) but as we show here expression markedly increases in axons within peripheral nerve and dorsal root.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the observation that Kv1.6 expression is stable in DRG but increases in axons.

claim: Altered α subunit composition and localisation of Kv1 channels is likely to have functional implications.
source: Altered α subunit composition and localisation of Kv1 channels is likely to have functional implications.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in Kv1 channel composition and distribution.

claim: In the naïve state, Kv1 channels located within the juxtaparanode have little functional impact on nodal excitability and conduction in peripheral nerves.
source: In the naïve state, the Kv1 channels Kv1.1 and 1.2 are located within the juxtaparanode, below the insulating myelin sheath and at least in peripheral nerves have little functional impact on nodal excitability and conduction (Poliak et al., 2003; Chiu and Ritchie, 1980; Sherratt et al., 1980; Rasband et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During development when Kv1 channels are observed in the node and paranode, specific blockers of this K current suggest that these Kv1 channels prevent re-entrant excitation in motor axons.
source: During development when Kv1 channels are observed in the node and paranode using specific blockers of this K current suggests that these Kv1 channels prevent re-entrant excitation in motor axons (Vabnick et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Following primary demyelination, the re-distribution of Kv1 channels to the paranode acts to suppress continuous conduction in demyelinated axons.
source: Following primary demyelination, the re-distribution of Kv1 channels to the paranode acts to suppress continuous conduction in demyelinated axons (Rasband et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The rate of ectopic activity within myelinated axons is very high in the first week and then decreases the longer the time elapsed following the initial injury.
